title: Erdős Problem #689: Double Covering by Prime Congruence Classes
description: For large n, can we choose a_p for each prime p ≤ n so that every m ∈ [1,n] satisfies m ≡ a_p (mod p) for at least 2 primes? Generalizes to r-fold covering. Open.

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Defines `primesUpTo n` as the Finset of primes $\leq n$, `IsCoveredBy m p a` as the congruence $m \equiv a \pmod{p}$, `coveringCount` as the number of primes covering $m$, and `IsRFoldCover n r a` requiring every $m \in [1,n]$ to be covered by $\geq r$ primes.

sections.title: Structural Properties
sections.summary: Proves five structural theorems: trivial nonnegativity of covering count, 0-fold covering for any assignment, monotonicity of coverage in $r$ (`isRFoldCover_le`), upper bound by $\pi(n)$ (`coveringCount_le_card_primes`), monotonicity in $n$ (`coveringCount_mono` and `isRFoldCover_primes_mono`).

sections.title: Small Cases
sections.summary: Proves `primesUpTo_one` ($\pi(1) = 0$, no primes $\leq 1$) and `coveringCount_one` (covering count is 0 when $n = 1$). These establish base cases showing coverage is impossible for very small $n$.

sections.title: Main Conjecture and Generalization
sections.summary: Axiomatizes `erdos_689_double_cover`: for large $n$, a 2-fold cover exists. Axiomatizes `erdos_689_r_fold`: for any fixed $r \geq 1$ and sufficiently large $n$, an $r$-fold cover exists.

sections.title: Connections and Supporting Results
sections.summary: Axiomatizes Mertens' theorem ($\sum_{p \leq n} 1/p \to \infty$), the Jacobsthal function connection (1-fold covering exists for large $n$, related to Problem #687), and Ben Green's variant asking for 10-fold coverage.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős posed this problem in 1979 [Er79d], asking whether prime congruence classes can doubly cover an interval. It belongs to the rich tradition of covering congruence problems that Erdős pioneered starting in the 1950s. Classical covering systems use arbitrary moduli to ensure every integer satisfies at least one congruence; here the moduli are restricted to primes $\leq n$. The key heuristic is Mertens' theorem (1874): $\sum_{p \leq n} 1/p \sim \log\log n$, so a random assignment of residue classes covers each integer $m$ by approximately $\log\log n$ primes on average. Since $\log\log n \to \infty$, double coverage is plausible but proving that the minimum coverage (over all $m$) reaches 2 is the challenge. The problem is related to Erdős Problems #687 and #688 on the Jacobsthal function and covering congruences, and to Hough's 2015 resolution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems with distinct odd moduli. Ben Green included the $r = 10$ variant as Problem 45 on his open problems list.
overview.problemStatement: For sufficiently large $n$, can we choose congruence classes $a_p$ for all primes $2 \leq p \leq n$ such that every integer $m \in [1,n]$ satisfies $m \equiv a_p \pmod{p}$ for at least 2 primes $p$?
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines $r$-fold covering precisely, then proves five structural properties (monotonicity in $r$ and $n$, trivial bounds, small cases) before stating the open conjectures. The key definitions use `Finset.filter` and `Finset.card` to count covering primes. Mertens' theorem and the Jacobsthal function connection are axiomatized to provide context for why the conjecture is believed true.
keyInsights: The average covering count per integer is $\sum_{p \leq n} 1/p \sim \log\log n$ by Mertens' theorem, which grows without bound but extremely slowly (e.g., $\log\log(10^{10}) \approx 3.1$)

The challenge is converting an average-case guarantee to a worst-case one: even though most integers are well-covered, ensuring every integer in $[1,n]$ reaches count $\geq 2$ requires careful choice of residue classes
Monotonicity in $r$ (`isRFoldCover_le`) and in $n$ (`coveringCount_mono`) are proved formally, showing the problem has a natural hierarchical structure
The 1-fold case (simple covering) follows from known results on the Jacobsthal function, so the real open content begins at $r = 2$
Ben Green's variant with threshold 10 instead of 2 highlights that even for moderate $r$, the problem remains open, despite $\log\log n$ eventually exceeding any fixed $r$

conclusion.summary: The formalization captures Erdős Problem 689 on double covering by prime congruence classes, with precise definitions, five proved structural theorems, and axiomatized open conjectures. The structural results (monotonicity, bounds, small cases) are fully proved with 0 sorries, while the main question, its generalization, and supporting number-theoretic facts are axiomatized.
conclusion.implications: Resolution would advance the theory of covering congruences with prime moduli, connecting to probabilistic combinatorics (Lovász Local Lemma applications), sieve methods, and the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions. The gap between average-case and worst-case behavior is a fundamental theme in combinatorial number theory, and new techniques here could apply to related problems on covering systems.
openQuestions: Does a 2-fold covering exist for all sufficiently large $n$? What is the smallest such $n$?
For what threshold $r_0$ does the Lovász Local Lemma suffice to prove $r$-fold covering for all $r \leq r_0$?
What is the minimum $n_0(r)$ such that $r$-fold covering is achievable for $n \geq n_0(r)$? Is $n_0(r)$ doubly exponential in $r$?
Can explicit (deterministic polynomial-time) constructions of covering assignments be found, or is the existence inherently probabilistic?

crossReferences.description: The prime density heuristic relies on the prime number theorem and Mertens' theorem for the sum of reciprocals of primes
The infinitude of primes ensures that more primes become available as n grows, making r-fold covering increasingly plausible
